README (start):
The open-source Devin alternative: a coding agent your team works with in Slack, on its own computers, in your cloud or ours.

  Cloud | Self-hosting | Docs | Website | Benchmark | Community | X

  
  

  

  
  
  

## Introduction

OpenComputer is the open source, self hostable alternative to Devin. Mention `@Computer` in a Slack thread with a task, it works on its own computer, you & your team can watch and steer it as it goes, and the result lands as a pull request.

It is open source from the compute layer up, so you can run all of it in your own cloud account, or start on OpenComputer Cloud in two minutes.

We built it to feel as fast as Claude Code on your laptop: in our benchmark it opens PRs 3.3x faster than Devin.

## See it work

  

## As fast as local

  

## How it works

OpenComputer is built to be simple to self-host without giving up scale or security. The whole stack runs on a single VM, which we recommend locking down to outbound-only network access.

The VM runs the gateway, Calvin: a thin bridge that listens for Slack events and starts a session with Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode, depending on your configuration. Each session is isolated with rootless Podman. Its state is written first to the VM's local disk, then persisted to a git-backed store.

The rest of the stack runs on Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects. Support for Fly and other platforms is coming soon.

  

## Try it in Cloud

The fastest way to experience `@Computer` is to install the Slack app from the cloud: [sign up here](https://app.opencomputer.dev), connect your repos, and install the Slack app to get started.

  

- **3.3x faster than Devin**: all 4 PRs open with CI green in 56s vs 185s ([benchmark](https://opencomputer.dev/blog/cloud-agents-as-fast-as-local/))
- **2.6x faster than the average of the 4 most popular cloud agents**: first push in 24s vs a 62s average ([benchmark](https://opencomputer.dev/blog/cloud-agents-as-fast-as-local/))
- **3-day free trial** with 600 work minutes
- **Bring your own ChatGPT / Codex subscription**

Agent Canvas

The self-hosted developer control center for coding agents and automations.

Run OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Pi, OpenCode, or any ACP-compatible agent across local, remote, and cloud backends.

   
Quickstart | Docs | Self-Hosting | ACP Agents | Automations | Slack

OpenHands Agent Canvas turns your coding agents into a self-hosted, always-on engineering team. It's a developer control center for starting conversations and automating everyday tasks — like generating reports that publish to Slack or automatically decomposing GitHub issues into tasks.

It runs locally on your machine by default, but can connect to multiple “agent backends”, e.g. running agents in Docker containers, on VMs, or within your company infrastructure. You can optionally choose to run agents on OpenHands Cloud or OpenHands Enterprise infrastructure.

Agent Canvas runs the open source OpenHands agent out-of-the-box, but can use third-party agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Pi, and OpenCode.

	
Self-host your way	Run agents locally, in Docker, on VMs, or anywhere you can run an agent server backend
Switch between different backends	Switch between local, remote, and cloud agents without losing focus
Create automations	Create automations and workflows that integrate with Slack, GitHub, Linear, and more. Run on a schedule or in response to webhook events
Integrate with the tools you use	Connect your automations with third-party services like Slack, GitHub, Notion, and more to automate workflows
Bring your own model	Use with any LLM
Use with any agent	Use with OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Pi, OpenCode, or any agent with Agent-Client Protocol (ACP).

If you have questions or feedback, please open a GitHub issue or join the #proj-agent-canvas channel in Slack.

Quickstart

You can install OpenHands to run agents on any machine: on your laptop, on a dedicated computer like a Mac Mini, or on a server in the cloud.

The most powerful way to run OpenHands is on a server in the cloud. This allows your agents to continue running even when your laptop is shut, and makes it easier to trigger your agents through third-party services like Slack, GitHub, and Datadog. See SELF_HOSTING.md for details, especially with respect to security hardening.

Notably, you can run the backend in multiple different environments, and switch between them from the same Agent Canvas frontend. E.g. you can share an Agent Server with your team for agents doing code review and dependency updates, then have your personal agents running on your laptop.

Option 1: Without a Sandbox

Warning

This runs the agent-server directly on the machine you're installing on — the agent will have full access to your filesystem!

Prerequisites: Node.js 24 or later, uv

npm install -g @openhands/agent-canvas
agent-canvas

The agent-canvas command starts the full local stack by default. You can also split it when you want to run pieces separately:

agent-canvas --frontend-only  # static frontend + ingress only
agent-canvas --backend-only   # agent server + automation backend + ingress only
Option 2: With a Docker Sandbox

Install Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows, or Docker Engine/Docker Desktop on Linux. Windows users can follow the PowerShell quickstart.

The steps below are for macOS and Linux. A named Docker volume stores settings, secrets, and conversations; projects are mounted at /projects.

1. Prepare a workspace

export PROJECTS_PATH="$HOME/projects"  # directory containing your project folders
mkdir -p "$PROJECTS_PATH"

On Linux Docker Engine, uid 10001 inside the container must be able to read and write the workspace and its existing files. Grant that user access using appropriate ownership or ACLs for your system. For a dedicated workspace you are comfortable sharing with all local users, the following is another option:

find "$PROJECTS_PATH" -type d -exec chmod a+rwX {} +
find "$PROJECTS_PATH" -type f -exec chmod a+rw {} +

These commands grant all host users access to the workspace. Keep it separate from ~/.openhands and other sensitive data. Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows handles bind-mount permissions, so those commands are normally unnecessary.

2. Start Agent Canvas

docker run -it --rm \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 \
  -e AGENT_CANVAS_ALLOW_LAN_SESSION_KEY=true \
  -v openhands-state:/home/openhands/.openhands \
  -v "${PROJECTS_PATH}:/projects" \
  ghcr.io/openhands/agent-canvas:1.43.0 # x-release-please-version

Open http://localhost:8000/canvas. Reuse openhands-state to retain state across container removals. A fresh volume does not contain existing ~/.openhands data; inspect or back it up with docker volume inspect openhands-state.

Linux permission troubleshooting and existing state

Note

The entrypoint stops the container with exit code 1 when the Agent Server stops answering its /alive check for about 30 seconds, so a crash or hang fails visibly instead of leaving a container that returns 502 for every request. Automatic recovery needs a restart policy: use --restart unless-stopped instead of --rm, or restart: unless-stopped in Docker Compose.

The agent will be able to access any project under PROJECTS_PATH.

Option 3: With Multiple Docker Sandboxes

Run each new conversation in its own Docker container, with its own Agent Server and tools. This is useful for running several agents concurrently. Canvas and the outer Agent Server run on your host and route conversation requests to the containers.

Prerequisites: Node.js 24 or later, uv, and a running Docker Desktop (macOS) or Docker Engine/Desktop (Linux). The user starting Canvas must be able to run docker commands.

macOS / Linux:

npm install -g @openhands/agent-canvas
OH_CONVERSATION_RUNTIME=docker agent-canvas

Open http://localhost:8000 and start a new conversation. Existing local conversations are not converted. Each container mounts its conversation's workspace and persisted state, so workspace files and conversation history survive container replacement. Conversations using the same host workspace still share those files; choose separate directories or worktrees to avoid conflicting edits.

This setting isolates conversation execution; it does not move the entire Canvas or automation service into a sandbox. For Windows, see README.windows.md.

Option 4: From Source

Warning

This runs the agent-server directly on the machine you're installing on — the agent will have full access to your filesystem!

Prerequisites: Node.js 24 or later, npm 11.12.1 (the repository pin), uv (for running the agent server via uvx)

Check npm --version before resolving dependencies. The seven-day release-age filter (npm install --min-release-age=7) requires npm >=11.10; older versions do not enforce it. Use npm ci to replay the committed lockfile. This npm requirement is for contributor dependency resolution, not for installing the published Canvas package.

git clone https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands.git
cd OpenHands
npm ci
npm run dev

Access the UI at http://localhost:8000 for the npm/source launchers, or http://localhost:8000/canvas for the Docker image. You can add additional backends directly from the UI.

Local (npx / npm run dev) listeners bind loopback only (127.0.0.1) so the auto-injected session key is not reachable from other machines on the network. To listen on all interfaces, pass --host 0.0.0.0 (or set OH_BIND_HOST); the session key is then not injected and the UI uses the same API-key entry screen as --public.

Docker listens on all container interfaces so port publishing works, but does not inject its session key into HTML by default. The quickstart above explicitly enables injection while publishing the host port on 127.0.0.1 only. If you publish Docker on a LAN or public interface, omit AGENT_CANVAS_ALLOW_LAN_SESSION_KEY and enter the API key in the UI. Set LOCAL_BACKEND_API_KEY to a strong value, or retrieve the generated value with docker exec <container> sh -c 'cat "$STATE_DIR/api-key.txt"'. For internet-facing installs, follow self-hosting.

Architecture

Agent Canvas is powered by the OpenHands Agent Server, a REST API for running multiple agents on a single machine. Each Agent Server runs on a single host/port; the Agent Canvas can connect to multiple Agent Servers and easily flip between them.

You can run an Agent Server anywhere:

Directly on your laptop (be careful!)
On a dedicated machine like a Mac Mini
On a virtual machine in the cloud
Inside OpenHands Cloud (our commercial offering)

The Agent Server is often paired with an Automation Server, which lets you set up agents that run on a schedule or in response to events.

Repository boundaries

Agent Canvas is part of a multi-repository OpenHands system. Changes should go to the repository that owns the behavior:

Repository	Responsibility
OpenHands/OpenHands	Agent Canvas frontend, user-facing control center, backend selection, and local-stack orchestration.
OpenHands/software-agent-sdk	Python SDK, Agent Server, agents, tools, conversations, workspaces, events, and the canonical server API.
OpenHands/typescript-client	Browser-compatible TypeScript client for the Agent Server API.
OpenHands/automation	Automation definitions, scheduling, webhooks, run history, and dispatching.

The Agent Server API is implemented by the SDK and consumed through the TypeScript client by Agent Canvas. The automation service decides when work runs and dispatches conversations to the Agent Server/SDK, which decides what runs. See AGENTS.md for contributor-specific boundaries and the required custom code-review guide.

## What happens when cloud agents are as fast as your local machine? – OpenComputer
URL: https://opencomputer.dev/blog/cloud-agents-as-fast-as-local/
Description: Cloud coding agents lost on interactivity, not capability. We built @computer to be as fast as Claude Code on your laptop, and benchmarked it against local Claude Code and other cloud coding agents.

BLOG

What happens when cloud agents are as fast as your local machine?

By Igor Zalutski, Mohamed Habib, Utpal Nadiger · October 30, 2026

We’ve spent the last few years obsessing over infrastructure. Over the last few months, we’ve been especially focused on cloud coding agents and on how to make it as easy as possible for developers transitioning from the local machines to continue using them without a problem.

In fact this attempt started internally in our team late last year, somewhere around the time when Andrej Karpathy wrote his “2025 LLM year in review”, article, we’ve basically been hammering at it ever since. To us, coding agents moving to a secure cloud environment seemed inevitable, but the question was why it had not happened yet?

The bottleneck is speed, we realized, and we thought, “What happens when cloud agents are as fast as your local machine?”

When you ping your favourite cloud coding agent in Slack with a task, for example, you don’t expect it to reply instantly. It would take a few seconds, maybe ask a clarifying question, then go away and produce a PR that you or another agent would glance over. We’re now used to equating cloud-based agents with “background agents”, as if it was the same thing. But it’s not.

With Claude Code running on your laptop you wouldn’t work this way. You can of course give it a goal and leave it unattended, and it’ll get it done - but that doesn’t work well for the most important work that you care about most. You’d typically first iterate on designs, plans, different approaches with lots of back-and-forth, look at some prototypes, and most importantly clarify what exactly it is that you want before throwing a swarm of agents at it.

This is the gap that is not (yet) well addressed with cloud agents.

We lose interactivity with background agents as of today!

And interactivity matters a lot, much more than it seems. The main reason is that context-switching is extremely expensive - it’s quite literally the worst possible way to use the human brain. An agent that takes just a tiny bit too long to respond forces you to switch to something else, and every switch costs your brain dearly. It’s a lot like token cache in LLMs actually, very similar dynamic. Except that imagine if cache misses in LLMs made them much slower and much dumber - that’s roughly what context-switching does to the human brain.

Another factor is wasted effort because of extended feedback loops. If you provide feedback to the agent as soon as there’s something to critique, it won’t waste any time. But if you only share feedback when the entire project is done, chances are that 90% of the work will be wasted and will need to be redone. So working with a slower agent is not merely slower proportionally to speed - the time to project completion grows non-linearly.

While models weren’t good enough we got used to agents other than those running on our laptops being too slow to be interactive - so we keep using them in fire-and-forget fashion. But all this does is grow work in progress for no reason, and overloading our brains. Full autonomy isn’t the answer either. As soon as full autonomy at some level is achieved, it stops being a concern for humans - it’s just done fully automatically, without any need to interact with it at all. You’d just switch your attention to a level above where AI still needs steering occasionally. And there, attention management matters again.

@Computer and how it happened

Since launching OpenComputer about seven weeks ago (after a few months in alpha), we kept seeing very similar patterns: many users were building cloud coding agents to use from Slack, and most were hacking them together on our agent API.

This prompted us to build @Computer, initially as a template. It would soon become our daily driver for writing code internally. But given its interactivity and speed, we decided to lead with it and benchmark it too, so users can easily try it in Slack.

Here’s what that looked like:

@Computer vs local Claude Code

Our first test was to compare an OpenComputer cloud session with a local Claude Code session side by side. In order to perform this test we built a CLI client for OpenComputer.

In a few rounds of tests of side by side comparison with the same task we saw that OpenComputer was either as fast as local Claude or faster. This test was run on a local MacBook Pro M2 machine. One of the surprising advantages of having a cloud session is that it is likely closer to the inference provider or colocated with it, which (to our surprise) also leads to sometimes faster than local speeds. In this video the left is Claude Code running on the local Mac machine, the right is opc running in a remote cloud session. Both have been given the same task in the same repo for a fair comparison.

@Computer vs other cloud coding agents

The second comparison we did was OpenComputer vs other cloud coding agents such as Devin (& friends). In order to test the speed of a task we created a simple test where we give an agent access to 4 different repos and gave each agent the same task:

@<Agent> bump zod to the latest version in sb-config-loader, sb-api-schema, sb-form-validator and sb-event-parser, run the checks, and open a PR in each.

The repo is public here: https://github.com/diggerhq/speedbench

For each one of these the prompt was shared in Slack, we measured the time from the prompt (Slack message timestamp) until the 4 PRs appeared. The time from initial message until PR appearing in GitHub is the elapsed time.

For each provider we did 5 rounds of this test. After each round we closed the open PRs and started over. In some cases the providers needed an additional nudge to run the benchmark test since they would refuse the task given that a closed PR exists (memory interference).

We measured the median across 5 rounds and recorded the results as shown below:

	FIRST PUSH	ALL 4 PRS OPEN, CI GREEN	RUNS COMPLETED
OpenComputer	24s	56s	5/6
Capy	55s	85s	5/5
Replicas	53s	87s	4/9
Hoplite	69s	95s	4/6
Devin	72s	185s	5/5
